body_markdown:
A few weeks ago, I took my overpowered 1985 Corvette to Grattan Raceway for an[open lapping day](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/my-corvette-had-a-rough-first-go-at-the-track-and-im-not-even-mad/) and brought it home broken. It has since been patched up but the patches are not all permanent, because that relatively short spell on track was perfectly timed to help make a few decisions about what the plan is moving forward. This car was always going to get suspension, steering, and brake work, but to be honest I had still been debating exactly which parts I wanted and exactly what I wanted the car to be. That has all been clarified.


This project was always going to take time. Years, in fact. The nature of the work, how much of it needed to be done, how much of it I wanted to do myself (all of it), and how much all of it would cost in time and money—all of that meant the smartest thing I could do was phase the project to keep from burning out or stalling with Corvette parts covering every square inch of my shop. This meant leaving some things alone, even when I know that a stock 41-year-old chassis is no match for a fresh-ish 400-horsepower V-8, late-model TREMEC six-speed, and new everything else in the drivetrain.


This car is now in regular driving rotation, but the project is not done.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


To be honest, my plan for this car was to do everything but body and paint. That’s a broad directive, I realize, with options from a straight restoration to full custom, and everything in between. After reading about a handful of similar builds, I had a decent idea of what I wanted, but the last five months of street driving and that one track trip taught me that what I had been planning likely would have left me wanting.


The original plan was to use the last 40 years of development to make the car into what I thought I needed. Instead, I’ve found that, much like last night’s dinner, my eyes are bigger than my stomach. My plan exceeded my capabilities, in other words. There are enough built C4 Corvettes in the wild to know I could build a really fast car if I selected, sourced, and installed the perfect combination of parts. I’ve come to understand that a really fast, stiff, aggressive car would likely not be fun for me. Not only that, but my driving skills would not be enough to extract what’s possible out of those high-performance parts. So why buy them at all?


Well, I’m not going to. Here’s what I *do* plan on doing with the three systems that still need attention on my tired-out Corvette:


## Steering


This system is already a mix of the factory fourth-generation Corvette steering rack and a fifth-generation steering pump. The rack is tired and needs help, as the all-to-common “morning sickness” has begun to lock up the steering when cold. The rack needs to be rebuilt, and I hope to also talk to an expert who might be able to tune or recommend a pump that could bolt to the front of the LS V-8 and provide the pressure and volume the factory rack wants so they can both live a long life.


That new steering wheel is attached to an aging rack that has started complaining.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


I initially thought this Corvette was optioned with the Z51 package, but after plenty of crawling under and around the car, I now know that is not the case. This means a rebuilt steering rack is easier to source, as the Z51 cars had a quicker steering ratio and are more desirable despite lower production. While I initially thought that quicker ratio might be a nice “upgrade,” I’ve run the numbers and thought hard about it and am willing to give up the half turn lock-to-lock difference to save a few dollars. Even during the four days of autocross I did, I never wanted for faster steering and strongly feel I have plenty of learning and progress to do before I would be able to tell the difference.


## Suspension


This rear suspension design can bind if the bushings don’t have enough flex.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Basically everything you see in this photo needs some type of attention, replacement, or repair.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Those rubber bushings have seen better days, and they were decades ago.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The overall condition of the chassis on this car is *tired* , but that doesn’t mean it is broken or malfunctioning. The rubber bushings, which keep the pivots and links that allow the chassis to float while the wheels move to absorb imperfections in the road, are cracked and misshapen. This allows significantly more movement than the engineers intended. The popular replacement are polyurethane bushings, which are significantly stiffer than the factory rubber but also break down relatively quickly, often squeak, and can create a bind in the rear suspension of the C4.


So I want rubber. Only problem is: rubber doesn’t exist. I’m currently shopping for solutions but likely will be sitting on a backorder list for a bit to get the right answer to my needs. Time will tell, but with winter right around the corner, it would be nice to get bushings right away so I could get started on the work ahead of next year’s driving season.


## Brakes


With the power I’ve got, it was easy to find myself pushing 120 mph going into turn one at Grattan Raceway. This was mostly due to me just getting carried away having fun, but every time the car was properly slowed down by parts store rotors and a set of EBC Bluestuff pads. It worked, and better than expected, which made me start to question my initial plan of adapting a set of fixed calipers from a later Corvette. But after going to a track day, I discovered that while I really enjoy “big” tracks on motorcycles, I would rather autocross a car. Thus, my braking needs fall closer to the stock end of the spectrum than I had previously been planning.


Those EBC pads were a nice step up from parts store bits, but a quality set of rotors will help even more.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


That grungy caliper deserves fresh seals and a good coat of paint.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The stock brakes proved to be enough for me, so might as well leave well enough alone. Kind of.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Fitting a quality set of rotors, rebuilding the calipers, and adding the right pads have proven to be everything I need and will leave more budget for actually getting out and driving the car, rather than having cool parts I don’t need to (potentially) impress people I don’t know at cars and coffee. This car isn’t built for bragging rights; it’s built to be fun to drive how I like to drive. Turns out this 41-year-old chassis is a lot closer to my wants than I expected. Just a little bit of refreshing—OK, a lot bit of a refreshing—and I expect to have a car that can all but hide in traffic and still put a huge smile on my face whenever I’m behind the wheel.


The phased approach to this project allowed me to take a step back and reassess my initial plan and parts list. The goal hasn’t changed, but it sure is nice to find out the path to what I desire is actually going to be a little easier than expected. Probably shouldn’t say that out loud, though…
